q-95099.name: Question 1
q-95099.problem:
Given that the random variable $X∼B(100,0.4),$ use the normal approximation to the binomial distribution to approximate $P(X=50).$ Give your final answer to three decimal places

*Hint: The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z)$ for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.04\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.9\,$ | $\,0.9738\,$ | $\,0.9744\,$ | $\,0.9750\,$ |
| $\,2.0\,$ | $\,0.9793\,$ | $\,0.9798\,$ | $\,0.9803\,$ |
| $\,2.1\,$ | $\,0.9838\,$ | $\,0.9842\,$ | $\,0.9846\,$ |
| $\,2.2\,$ | $\,0.9875\,$ | $\,0.9878\,$ | $\,0.9881\,$ |
| $\,2.3\,$ | $\,0.9904\,$ | $\,0.9906\,$ | $\,0.9909\,$ |
q-95099.worked_solution:
Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=100$ and $p=0.4.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =100\cdot 0.4 \\  & =40 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =100\cdot (1-0.4) \\  & =60 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(100)(0.4)=40
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(100)(0.4)(1-0.4)=24.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(40,24).$

Now, we can approximate the desired probability $P(X=50).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(X=50)≈P(49.5\le Y\le 50.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(49.5\le Y\le 50.5) & =P(\frac{49.5-40}{\sqrt{24}}\le Z\le \frac{50.5-40}{\sqrt{24}}) \\  & ≈P(1.94\le Z\le 2.14) \\  & =P(Z\le 2.14)-P(Z<1.94) \\  & =P(Z\le 2.14)-P(Z\le 1.94) \\  & =Φ(2.14)-Φ(1.94) \\  & =0.9838-0.9738 \\  & =0.010\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(X=50)≈0.010.
$$

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.0102.$

q-95722.name: Question 2
q-95722.problem:
Which of the following probabilities could be approximated using the normal approximation of the binomial distribution?

I. The probability that a student correctly solves $4$ questions in a $5$-question math test if the student has a $75%$ probability of correctly answering each question.

II. The probability that $42$ flights out of $120$ arrive early at an airport if the probability of a single flight arriving early is $0.45$ for each flight.

III. The probability of getting $4$ ones on $10$ rolls of a $4$-sided die.
q-95722.worked_solution:
Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Let's now examine each situation.

- In situation I, we have $n=5$ and $p=0.75.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =5\cdot 0.75 \\  & =3.75 \\  & ≯5.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, we *cannot* use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

- In situation II, we have $n=120$ and $p=0.45.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =120\cdot 0.45 \\  & =54 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =120\cdot (1-0.45) \\  & =66 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

- In situation III, we have $n=10$ and $p=\frac{1}{4}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =10\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =2.5 \\  & ≯5.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, we *cannot* use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

q-95757.name: Question 3
q-95757.problem:
An archer practices firing an arrow at a target $60$ times. The archer has a $44%$ chance of hitting the bull's eye. Using the normal approximation to the binomial distribution, estimate the probability that the archer hits the bull's eye more than $30$ times. Give your final answer to three decimal places.

*Hint: The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z)$ for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.9\,$ | $\,0.8289\,$ | $\,0.8315\,$ | $\,0.8340\,$ |
| $\,1.0\,$ | $\,0.8531\,$ | $\,0.8554\,$ | $\,0.8577\,$ |
| $\,1.1\,$ | $\,0.8749\,$ | $\,0.8770\,$ | $\,0.8790\,$ |
q-95757.worked_solution:
Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=60$ and $p=0.44.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =60\cdot 0.44 \\  & =26.4 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =60\cdot (1-0.44) \\  & =33.6 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(60)(0.44)=26.4
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(60)(0.44)(1-0.44)=14.784.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(26.4,14.784).$

Now, we can estimate the desired probability $P(X>30).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(X>30)=P(X\ge 31)≈P(Y\ge 30.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\ge 30.5) & =P(Z\ge \frac{30.5-26.4}{\sqrt{14.784}}) \\  & ≈P(Z\ge 1.07) \\  & =1-P(Z<1.07) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 1.07) \\  & =1-Φ(1.07) \\  & =1-0.8577 \\  & =0.1423\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(X>30)≈0.142.
$$

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.1431.$

$$

q-132293.html:
Question 4
?

Using the normal approximation to the binomial distribution, approximate the probability of getting 30 odd numbers on 70 rolls of a 6-sided die. Give your final answer to three decimal places.

Hint: The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function Φ(z) for the standard normal distribution.

z0.000.010.02
−1.3 0.0968 0.0951 0.0934
−1.2 0.1151 0.1131 0.1112
−1.1 0.1357 0.1335 0.1314
−1.0 0.1587 0.1562 0.1539
z0.070.080.09
−1.3 0.0854 0.0838 0.0823
−1.2 0.1020 0.1003 0.0985
−1.1 0.1210 0.1190 0.1170
−1.0 0.1423 0.1401 0.1379
a
0.040
b

Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a binomial random variable X∼B(n,p), if

  • np>5, and

  • n(1−p)>5,

we can approximate X as a normal random variable Y with mean μ=np and variance σ2=np(1−p), that is,

Y∼N(np,np(1−p)).

Here, we have n=70 and p=0.5. Therefore, np=70⋅0.5=35>5✓n(1−p)=70⋅(1−0.5)=35>5.✓ So, we can approximate our binomial random variable X with a normal random variable Y with mean

μ=np=(70)(0.5)=35

and variance

σ2=np(1−p)=(70)(0.5)(1−0.5)=17.5.

That is, we can approximate X by Y∼N(35,17.5).

Now, we can approximate the desired probability P(X=30). Using a continuity correction, we have

P(X=30)≈P(29.5≤Y≤30.5).

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by z-scoring:

P(29.5≤Y≤30.5)=P(29.5−3517.5≤Z≤30.5−3517.5)≈P(−1.31≤Z≤−1.08)=P(Z≤−1.08)−P(Z<−1.31)=P(Z≤−1.08)−P(Z≤−1.31)=Φ(−1.08)−Φ(−1.31)=0.1401−0.0951=0.045

Therefore,

P(X=30)≈0.045.

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of 0.0469.

q-132494.worked_solution:
Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=100$ and $p=0.5.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =100\cdot 0.5 \\  & =50 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =100\cdot (1-0.5) \\  & =50 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(100)(0.5)=50
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(100)(0.5)(1-0.5)=25.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(50,25).$

Now, we can estimate the desired probability $P(43<X<53).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(43<X<53)=P(44\le X\le 52)≈P(43.5\le Y\le 52.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(43.5\le Y\le 52.5) & =P(\frac{43.5-50}{\sqrt{25}}\le Z\le \frac{52.5-50}{\sqrt{25}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.30\le Z\le 0.50) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.50)-P(Z<-1.30) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.50)-P(Z\le -1.30) \\  & =Φ(0.50)-Φ(-1.30) \\  & =0.6915-0.0968 \\  & =0.5947\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(43<X<53)≈0.595.
$$

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.5947.$
